source.title: Standard SAEs Might Be Incoherent: A Choosing Problem & A “Concise” Solution

record.tranche_reason: The post argues that standard SAE explanations can be non-unique and illustrates this with a Gemma Scope example, challenging the idea that SAE features provide canonical explanations.
record.gate_note: The post also discusses superposition as background, but does not test its geometry or capacity account. The hypothetical MDL activation distributions are not reported as empirical results. The Gemma Scope example is an illustrative case, not a systematic evaluation.
record.test_reason: The post argues that a standard SAE dictionary admits several equally sparse, equally accurate decompositions of one activation, so explanations built from them are not canonical. It gives one Gemma Scope example. This bears on the 'canonical units' part of V5. The argument is mostly analytic, with one real-model illustration.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that standard SAEs (L0+MSE) do not pick a unique explanatory mediator, so feature-based explanations are ill-defined. They propose MDL-SAEs as a more principled choice but not the only one. Their stated practical impact for SAE users is 'probably nothing dramatic'.
record.recipe_differences: The post analyzes ambiguity in SAE explanations and gives an illustrative Gemma Scope case; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.problems: The real-model evidence is a single illustrative example with an approximate feature relation; there is no systematic sample, control, or quantified uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying results. The post’s hypothetical MDL activation-magnitude example is illustrative rather than an empirical result.

untested.parts: Completeness of SAE features; stability across seeds, widths or datasets; whether the dictionary directions themselves (rather than activation decompositions given a fixed dictionary) are canonical.
Not tested: no toy-model geometry or sparsity transition.
Not tested: SAE use is assumed, not evaluated as evidence of sparse features.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is mostly theoretical. The real-model case is one approximate example found in minutes of search. The authors expect the problem to be worse for larger SAEs and larger k, but do not measure this. The MDL activation-distribution example is hypothetical (α=3) and correctly left out. I chose limits_scope rather than challenges for V5 because the post addresses non-uniqueness of activation decompositions under a fixed dictionary, not the canonicity of the features themselves, and it gives no quantified rate.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test feature storage geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometric arrangements in toy networks.
Does not test whether feature competition for capacity explains polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Does not measure feature distribution across neurons or establish that SAEs recover sparse features in LLMs.
Tests whether SAE feature explanations are canonical for the illustrated decompositions; does not assess completeness or stability across models, datasets, or training runs.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Constructed an overcomplete feature dictionary with two distinct sparse activation vectors decoding to the same neural activation.
rows.measure: Whether the same neural activation has a unique minimal explanatory mediator under reconstruction and sparsity criteria.
rows.value: Both z and z' decode to the same x and have L0=2.
rows.locator: Section 2, example with f1, f2, f3
rows.note: An analytic counterexample to uniqueness under the stated reconstruction and sparsity criteria.
rows.check: This is a hand-built mathematical counterexample, not a measurement of any trained system; subject_kind 'toy_network' is wrong. It is the post's argument rather than an empirical result, so it should not anchor a verdict on its own. Keep it as context or drop it as a row.

rows.subject: Gemma 2
rows.operation_detail: Compared approximate sparse decompositions and their Neuronpedia AutoInterp explanations using Gemma Scope SAE features.
rows.measure: Whether alternative approximate mediators for the same activation yield consistent semantic explanations.
rows.value: The explanation via z=(f1,f2) is described in terms of symbols; via z'=(f1,f3), it is described in terms of expressing inability in language.
rows.locator: Section 2, “Incoherency in the Wild with Gemma Scope”
rows.note: The post describes the decompositions as approximately minimal explanatory mediators for the same x; this is one illustrative example.
rows.check: The subject should be Gemma 2 2B residual stream, layer 16 (per the Neuronpedia URLs), not just 'Gemma 2'. The relation f3≈f2−0.01·f1 holds only approximately, and the reconstruction or approximation error is not quantified. This is one example from a brief, unoptimised search, with no baseline or control.
